summary: This document revises, extends, and replaces RFC 6622. It describes flexible TLVs for cryptographic Integrity Check Values and timestamps, using the MANET packet and message format from RFC 5444. It defines Packet, Message, and Address Block TLVs.

plainLanguage.summary: A mobile ad hoc network is a set of routers that talk to each other without a fixed central network. This document defines two small boxes that can be attached to a routing packet, a routing message or a list of addresses: one carries a tamper check and the other carries a timestamp. It also says exactly which bytes the tamper check covers, including how to handle the fields that change while a message travels.

subtitle: How a mobile ad hoc network carries a tamper check and a timestamp inside its routing packets and messages.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols for mobile ad hoc networks need a way to carry a tamper check and a timestamp, but the packet format they share leaves little room and the fields that change in flight complicate any check.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines two TLV types, ICV and TIMESTAMP, for packets, messages and address blocks, plus type extensions that say how the value field is built: a hash function code, a cryptographic function code, an optional key identifier and the check value itself.
tldr.outcome: This document replaced RFC 6622 and added a third ICV type extension that also covers the source address of the IP datagram, which matters for protocols that identify neighbours by that address.

sections.title: What the Specification Provides
sections.content:
This document specifies a syntactical representation of security-related information for use with the addresses, messages and packets of RFC 5444. It also specifies IANA registrations of TLV types and type extension registries for these TLV types. It is not a stand-alone protocol; it is intended for use by MANET routing protocols or by security extensions of them.

The document revises, extends and replaces RFC 6622. It specifies two kinds of TLV, one carrying Integrity Check Values (ICVs) and one carrying timestamps, in packets, messages and Address Blocks; a generic framework for using these TLVs that accounts for the specific features of Packet, Message and Address Block TLVs; and IANA registrations for TLVs and registries for TLV type extensions, replacing those from RFC 6622. It also specifies registries for code points for ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs, timestamps, hash functions and cryptographic functions.

Section 12 of the document defines a method for generating ICVs by combining a cryptographic function and a hash function, and for including such ICVs in the value field of a TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: This document says how to attach a tamper check and a timestamp to the routing packets and messages that a mobile ad hoc network exchanges. It fixes the shape of the boxes and the list of registered codes, so that different vendors can interoperate.

sections.title: The MANET Security Architecture
sections.content:
MANET routing protocol specifications may have a clause allowing a control message to be rejected as badly formed or insecure before it is processed or forwarded. Protocols such as the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) of RFC 6130 and the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 of RFC 7181 recognise external reasons, such as failure to verify an ICV, for rejecting a message.

This arrangement comes from the observation that with respect to security in MANETs one size rarely fits all, and that deployment domains have security requirements ranging from unbreakable to virtually none. The virtue of the approach is that the routing protocol specifications and their implementations can stay generic, with extensions providing security mechanisms specific to a deployment domain.

The architecture has three parts: routing protocol specifications, each with a clause allowing an extension to reject a message as badly formed or insecure; routing protocol security extensions, each rejecting messages as appropriate for a given security requirement; and code points and an exchange format for the information those extensions need. This document addresses the third part, by specifying a common exchange format for cryptographic ICVs and timestamps and reserving entries in the Packet TLV, Message TLV and Address Block TLV registries of RFC 5444 for use by MANET routing protocol security extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing protocols themselves stay general, so a network operator can add the level of security the site needs. This document supplies the shared pieces those extensions use: the boxes, the codes inside them and the registries that hold the codes.

sections.title: The ICV and Timestamp TLV Structure
sections.content:
The value of an ICV TLV is a sequence of one or more ICV values. Each ICV value is a field of length octets, except in a multivalue Address Block TLV where each is single-length octets, and it holds the information interpreted by the ICV verification process as specified by the type extension. The general structure does not say how to calculate the ICV value or what internal structure it has; the type extension must specify that.

The value of a Timestamp TLV is a sequence of one or more time values, each of length octets, or single-length octets in a multivalue Address Block TLV, and each holding a timestamp. Again, the type extension specifies how the time value is produced and how it is interpreted.

A timestamp is essentially freshness information. Its setting and interpretation are left to the MANET routing protocol or extension that uses it, and may for example be a POSIX timestamp, a GPS timestamp or a simple sequence number. Keeping time synchronised in a MANET may be difficult, because the architecture is decentralised and the topology is highly dynamic because of mobility and other factors, so specifying a time synchronisation mechanism is out of scope for this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box holds one or more values. The ICV box holds a check value, and the timestamp box holds a time value. How each value is produced and read is decided by the type extension, which is a number the document registers.

sections.title: Calculating the ICV for Packets, Messages and Addresses
sections.content:
Two Packet TLVs are defined: an ICV Packet TLV carrying the cryptographic ICV of a packet, and a TIMESTAMP Packet TLV carrying the time at which the ICV was calculated. Packets as defined in RFC 5444 are never forwarded by routers, so no special treatment is needed for the mutable fields, the hop count and hop limit, when calculating a packet ICV. Any ICV Packet TLVs already present must be removed before the ICV is calculated, and the Packet TLV Block size recalculated. If the block then holds no TLVs, the block must be removed and the phastlv bit in the packet header cleared. The removed ICV TLVs are restored afterwards and the block size recalculated again. If there is then no Packet TLV Block, one must be added and the phastlv bit set. The reason for removing the old ICV TLVs first is that several ICV TLVs may be added to the same packet, for example using different cryptographic or hash functions. The reason for removing an empty block is that a receiver cannot tell an absent Packet TLV Block from an empty one when it removes the ICV TLV to verify it.

If a packet contains TIMESTAMP TLVs and ICV TLVs, the TIMESTAMP TLVs, and any other Packet TLVs, must be added before the ICV TLVs, so that the timestamps and the other TLVs are covered by the ICV calculation.

For messages, the ICV Message TLV works the same way, with one extra rule: the hop limit and hop count fields in the Message Header, if present, must both be assumed to be zero when the ICV is calculated, because they change as the message is forwarded. Any ICV Message TLVs already present must be removed before calculating, and all other relevant TLVs must be added first so that they are covered. The removed ICV TLVs are restored afterwards, and the message size and Message TLV Block size recalculated.

For Address Blocks, the ICV is calculated over one or more addresses concatenated with any other values associated with those addresses, for example other Address Block TLV value fields. A protocol using ICV Address Block TLVs must specify how those extra values are included in the calculation and verification. The TLVs concatenated with the addresses must not be ICV Address Block TLVs already associated with those addresses, because several ICVs may be attached to the same address and the recipient does not know the order they were added in. If TIMESTAMP TLVs are associated with an address, their time values must be included before the ICV is calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the check value is worked out, the old check box is taken out of the packet and the length fields are adjusted, then the box is put back afterwards. That way several different check values can travel in the same packet. For messages, the hop count and hop limit are counted as zero, because those numbers change on the way.

sections.title: The ICV Value Field and Type Extensions
sections.content:
A common way to calculate an ICV combines a cryptographic function and a hash function applied to the content. This section specifies that decomposition, using type extension 1 or type extension 2 of the ICV TLVs.

The value of an ICV TLV with type extension 1 or 2 is made of a one-octet hash function field, a one-octet cryptographic function field, a one-octet key identifier length field, an optional key identifier field, and the ICV data. The key identifier length of zero is reserved for a single pre-installed shared key, in which case the key identifier field is not present. The ICV data field has a length of length minus 3 minus the key identifier length.

The calculation is assumed to decompose as ICV-value = cryptographic-function(hash-function(content)), although other combinations may be specified; that is the case for HMAC, which uses the hash function twice. A cryptographic function of none is provided for symmetry and possible future use, but should not be used with any currently specified hash function.

The ICV data field may be truncated after it is calculated, and the length indicates that it was. The truncation must follow the rules of the cryptographic function in use, and the minimal ICV length guidelines of NIST SP 800-107 apply, so that an ICV using HMAC is never truncated below 4 octets. The truncated length must be large enough that a dictionary attack has an acceptably small chance of success. With a length of L bits, 2 to the power L packets are needed for an attack with certainty of success; with a verification rate of R packets per second over N routers for an available time T, the probability of success is NRT/2 to the power L. For that not to exceed a probability P, L must be greater than log2(NRT/P). The document's example: with N of 32, R of 1000, T of 86400 seconds and P of 10 to the power -6, L must be at least 52 bits.

Some of the cryptographic and hash functions require the length of the content to be signed to be a multiple of a certain number of octets, so they specify padding mechanisms, such as AES-CMAC in RFC 4493, which pads message lengths that are not a multiple of 16 octets. Implementations of this framework must support the padding mechanisms the cryptographic or hash function specifications call for.
sections.plainLanguage: The value field names the hash function and the cryptographic function used, then optionally names the key, then holds the check value itself. The check value may be shortened, but not below the length that keeps an attacker's chance of guessing it small.

sections.title: Exactly What the ICV Covers
sections.content:
For type extension 1, the ICV of a packet is calculated over the hash function field, the cryptographic function field, the key identifier length field and, if present, the key identifier, in that order, followed by the entire packet, including the Packet Header, all Packet TLVs other than ICV Packet TLVs, and all included messages. For a message, the same fields are followed by the entire message. For one or more addresses, the same fields are followed by the addresses and then by any other values associated with those addresses.

Type extension 2 works the same way, except that the data covered also includes the source address of the IP datagram carrying the packet, message or Address Block. The source address is represented by a single octet holding the address length in octets, followed by that many octets holding the address in network byte order.

The reason for adding type extension 2 is that some MANET protocols, such as RFC 6130, use the IP source address of the datagram carrying the packet, message or Address Block, for example to identify links with neighbouring routers. If that address is not otherwise in the payload, it is not protected against tampering. This applies only to packets, which travel one hop, and to messages and their Address Blocks that travel one hop. It does not apply to messages that may be forwarded more than one hop, such as Topology Control messages in RFC 7181.
sections.plainLanguage: Type extension 1 protects the packet, message or address as sent. Type extension 2 also protects the address of the machine that sent it, so a neighbour cannot be swapped out. That only works for things that travel a single hop, because a forwarded message changes sender on the way.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The document creates IANA registries for the TLV types and for their type extensions. From the Packet TLV Types, Message TLV Types and Address Block TLV Types namespaces of RFC 5444, type 5 is ICV and type 6 is TIMESTAMP.

The type extension registries for ICV TLVs assign 0 to a plain ICV with no predefined internal structure, 1 to an ICV built from a cryptographic function and a hash function, and 2 to the same thing with the IP datagram source address included. Values 3 to 251 are unassigned and go through Expert Review, and 252 to 255 are reserved for experimental use. More than one ICV TLV with the same type extension may be included when they represent different calculations, such as different cryptographic or hash functions or a different key identifier, but ICV TLVs that declare the same information must not be included together.

The TIMESTAMP type extension registries assign 0 to an unsigned timestamp of arbitrary length whose interpretation the routing protocol must define, 1 to an unsigned 32-bit timestamp as in POSIX, 2 to the NTP timestamp format, and 3 to a signed timestamp of arbitrary length with no constraints such as monotonicity. More than one TIMESTAMP TLV with the same type extension must not be included in the same packet or message.

The hash function registry assigns 0 to none, the identity function where the hash value of an object is the object itself, 1 to SHA-1, 2 to SHA-224, 3 to SHA-256, 4 to SHA-384 and 5 to SHA-512. The cryptographic function registry assigns 0 to none, 1 to RSA, 2 to DSA, 3 to HMAC, 4 to 3DES, 5 to AES and 6 to ECDSA. In both registries the remaining values follow the same allocation policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers for these boxes, and the numbers for the hash and cryptographic functions inside them, were written into official lists so that each means the same thing everywhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document does not specify a protocol. It provides a syntactical component for the cryptographic ICVs of messages and packets, and can be used to address security issues of a MANET routing protocol or extension. It therefore has the same security considerations as RFC 5444.

A MANET routing protocol or extension that uses this specification must specify how to use the framework and the TLVs, and must describe the protection it thereby attains. As an example, a protocol that rejects badly formed or insecure messages when a control message has no valid ICV should state the security assumption that a valid ICV means the message is considered valid. It should also state the security issues this counteracts, such as link or identity spoofing, and the issues it does not counteract, such as compromised keys.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives the building blocks, not a complete protection scheme. The protocol that uses it has to say what it protects against and what it does not, for example that a stolen key still defeats the check.

fields.name: Hash Function
fields.desc: One octet naming the hash function that was used.

fields.name: Cryptographic Function
fields.desc: One octet naming the cryptographic function that was used.

fields.name: Key ID Length
fields.desc: Length of the key identifier in octets. Zero means a single pre-installed shared key.

fields.name: Key Identifier
fields.desc: Names the key used, so the receiver knows which key to check with.

fields.name: ICV Data
fields.desc: The cryptographic ICV itself. It may be truncated, but never below the length the guidelines require.

cells: The hash and function codes, the key identifier, and the packet, message or address
The same, plus the source address of the IP datagram
